sb_prompt: DOES YOUR FAMILY KEEP A MONTHLY BUDGETCAN YOU GIVE A GENERAL DESCRIPTION OF YOUR PROCEDURES
raw_output:
ParticipantA: Hello!
ParticipantB: Hello!
ParticipantA: Can I ask you something real quick? Does your family actually keep a monthly budget?
ParticipantB: Yeah, we do. Mostly just on paper, we write it down at the end of the month.
ParticipantA: Oh, really? Just at the end? Like to see where the money went?
ParticipantB: Yeah. Sometimes we can't even find the checkbook later, so it's pretty rough. But we try.
ParticipantA: I guess we kind of did that once, maybe ten years ago.
ParticipantB: Ten years? Wow, that's a while back.
ParticipantA: Yeah. My wife and I tried to make a spreadsheet on the computer.
ParticipantB: And what happened with that?
ParticipantA: Honestly? We kind of stopped doing it after a few months.
ParticipantB: Really? Why did you stop?
ParticipantA: I don't really know. We just kind of lost the habit, I guess. It felt like too much work for us.
ParticipantB: Too much work? That's weird, because I thought budgets kept you from spending too much.
ParticipantA: Well, it did help us save a little bit at first, but then it started feeling like we were just living paycheck to paycheck anyway, even with the budget.
ParticipantB: Oh, I see. That's actually pretty common. My cousin lived in the city once and he tried that too.
ParticipantA: Oh, really? Did it work for him?
ParticipantB: Not really. He made a budget, and then he just found ways to get around it, you know? Like buying things on credit or skipping meals.
ParticipantA: That sounds familiar. My wife would make the list, and then I'd buy something extra on Saturday, and by Sunday, the whole thing was gone.
ParticipantB: Yeah, it's like the plan doesn't account for the "fun stuff."
ParticipantA: Exactly. It felt like we were just tracking our own failures, you know?
ParticipantB: Yeah, that's what I think too. If you stress too much about every dollar, it takes the joy out of spending it.
ParticipantA: That's a good way to put it. I guess we just gave up on it years ago because of that.
ParticipantB: I think so. I mean, we look at our spending later, but we don't make a strict plan beforehand. Just sort of see how we did at the end of the month.
ParticipantA: That makes sense. I never really understood why people stuck to them so rigidly.
ParticipantB: Maybe because they don't have a choice? Some people have to budget because they can't afford anything else.
ParticipantA: That's true. We're lucky enough that we don't *have* to, even if we *could* benefit from it sometimes.
ParticipantB: Yeah, but for us, if we budget, we'd have to cut back on things we actually need, not just want.
ParticipantA: Oh, like what?
ParticipantB: Like, my daughter needs to buy new boots this winter. If we had a tight budget, we'd have to wait until next summer or something.
ParticipantA: Ugh, that sounds tough. I'd probably feel bad about letting her wait.
ParticipantB: Yeah, it's hard. But then again, if we didn't watch it at all, we'd be in trouble by November.
ParticipantA: Right. It's a fine line.
ParticipantB: Yeah. So, do you think we should try a little lighter version? Just track the big stuff?
ParticipantA: Maybe. I never thought about tracking just the big expenses. Maybe that would be enough.
ParticipantB: Yeah, maybe just the car payments and groceries and the kids' stuff.
ParticipantA: That sounds manageable. I might try that next month, just to see.
ParticipantB: Okay. Maybe we'll see.
ParticipantA: Sure. Well, thanks for talking.
ParticipantB: You too. Good luck with whatever you decide.
ParticipantA: Thanks. Bye.
ParticipantB: Bye.
